questions.question: State the cell theory. Who proposed it, and what are its exceptions?
questions.solution:
**Schleiden & Schwann (1838–39), extended by Virchow (1855):** (1) all living things are made of cells; (2) the cell is the structural and functional unit; (3) all cells arise from pre-existing cells (*omnis cellula e cellula*).

**Exceptions:** viruses (acellular), multinucleate coenocytes, and mitochondria/chloroplasts (their own DNA, endosymbiotic origin).
questions.knowledgeNote: Virchow's 'omnis cellula e cellula' killed spontaneous generation — the theory's third, decisive line.
questions.answer: **Cell theory:** (1) all living organisms are composed of **one or more cells**; (2) the **cell is the basic unit of structure and function** in all organisms; (3) **all cells arise from pre-existing cells** by division (Omnis cellula e cellula). **Proposed by:** **Matthias Schleiden** (plants, 1838) and **Theodor Schwann** (animals, 1839) for the first two points; **Rudolf Virchow** added the third in 1855. **Exceptions:** **viruses** (no cellular organisation — acellular); some organisms lack organelles such as mitochondria (e.g. mature mammalian **red blood cells** have no nucleus and most organelles); **skeletal muscle fibres** and some fungal hyphae are **multinucleate syncytia** (many nuclei in one cell mass). **Deep point:** the exceptions are instructive, not fatal — viruses and RBCs show what a cell *needs* to be alive, and their departures from the norm sharpen the theory's definition of the cell as the minimal self-replicating unit of life.

questions.question: What is binomial nomenclature? Write its any four rules with an example.
questions.solution:
**Binomial nomenclature** (Linnaeus, 1753) names each species with genus + species epithet.

Rules: (1) Latinised; (2) genus capitalised, species lowercase; (3) italicised in print, underlined separately by hand; (4) author cited on first use. **Example:** *Homo sapiens* L. — mango *Mangifera indica*.
questions.knowledgeNote: One scientific name worldwide ends the confusion of local names — the practical point behind the system.
questions.answer: **Binomial nomenclature:** the system of naming each species with **two words** — the **generic name (genus)** first and the **specific epithet (species)** second — introduced by **Carolus Linnaeus** (Species Plantarum, 1753). *Example:* *Mangifera indica* (mango), *Homo sapiens* (man). **Four rules:** (1) the name is in **Latin or latinised** form and is printed in **italics** (underlined when handwritten); (2) the **genus name begins with a capital letter**, the species name with a **small letter**; (3) each name is unique — no two species may share the same binomial; (4) the name, once validly published, has priority and can only be changed by the rules of the code (ICZN/ICBN); the author's name may be cited after the binomial (e.g. *Mangifera indica* Linn.). **Deep point:** two words do the work of a passport — the genus groups relatives, the species epithet singles out one kind, and the same binomial means the same organism everywhere in the world, ending the chaos of local common names.

questions.question: What is taxonomy? Describe the taxonomic hierarchy with an example.
questions.solution:
**Taxonomy** is the science of identifying, naming, and classifying organisms.

Hierarchy (broad → narrow): Kingdom → Phylum/Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. **Human:** Animalia → Chordata → Mammalia → Primates → Hominidae → *Homo* → *sapiens*.
questions.knowledgeNote: 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup' — the standard mnemonic for the seven ranks.
questions.answer: **Taxonomy:** the branch of biology concerned with the **identification, nomenclature and classification** of organisms — placing every known species into an ordered system based on natural relationships. **Taxonomic hierarchy (highest to lowest):** **Kingdom → Phylum/Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species** (memory aid: *King Philip Came Over For Good Soup*). Each rank is a **taxon**; a species is the basic and lowest unit. **Example (man):** Kingdom Animalia → Phylum Chordata → Class Mammalia → Order Primates → Family Hominidae → Genus *Homo* → Species *sapiens*. **Deep point:** the hierarchy is nested boxes — each higher rank contains all the lower ones; moving up the ladder the group gets more general and more inclusive, moving down more specific and more closely related.

questions.question: On what criteria did Whittaker classify organisms into five kingdoms? Name the kingdoms.
questions.solution:
**Criteria (1969):** cell type (prokaryotic/eukaryotic), body organisation (uni-/multicellular), nutrition (autotrophic/heterotrophic), and reproduction.

**Kingdoms:** Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
questions.knowledgeNote: Fungi earned independence by absorptive nutrition + chitin walls — neither plant nor animal.
questions.answer: **Whittaker's criteria (1969):** organisms were classified on **(1) cellular organisation** (prokaryote vs eukaryote; unicellular vs multicellular), **(2) mode of nutrition** (autotrophic — photosynthetic or chemosynthetic; heterotrophic — absorptive or ingestive), and (3) body organisation/thallus structure. **The five kingdoms:** **(1) Monera** — prokaryotes (bacteria, cyanobacteria); **(2) Protista** — unicellular eukaryotes (Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas); **(3) Fungi** — absorptive heterotrophs with chitinous cell walls (mushrooms, Mucor); **(4) Plantae** — multicellular photosynthetic autotrophs (mosses, ferns, flowering plants); **(5) Animalia** — multicellular ingestive heterotrophs without cell walls (sponges to mammals). **Deep point:** nutrition is the sharpest knife in Whittaker's scheme — the same three-way split (make food / absorb food / ingest food) separates plants, fungi and animals; prokaryote vs eukaryote is what isolates Monera.

questions.question: Write any four branches of biology and what each studies.
questions.solution: **Morphology** — form and structure. **Physiology** — life functions. **Genetics** — heredity and variation. **Ecology** — organisms and environment. (Also: cytology/cells, taxonomy/classification, microbiology/microbes, embryology/development.)
questions.knowledgeNote: Morphology (what it looks like) vs anatomy (dissected structure) vs physiology (what it does) — the classic trio.
questions.answer: **Four branches of biology:** (1) **Genetics** — heredity and variation; studies how traits pass from parents to offspring (e.g. why a child has the father's eye colour). (2) **Ecology** — organisms and their environment; studies populations, communities, ecosystems (e.g. how a forest food web responds to deforestation). (3) **Microbiology** — microorganisms; studies bacteria, viruses, fungi (e.g. how *E. coli* causes diarrhoea). (4) **Physiology** — the working of organs and systems; studies functions like digestion, respiration, nerve conduction (e.g. how the frog's heart maintains circulation). (Others: taxonomy, morphology, anatomy, embryology, molecular biology, biotechnology.) **Deep point:** each branch answers a different question about the same life — *what* (taxonomy), *how it works* (physiology), *how it inherits* (genetics), *how it lives with others* (ecology).

questions.question: Describe the steps of the scientific method in biological investigation.
questions.solution: Observation → question → **hypothesis** (testable explanation) → controlled **experiment** → data analysis → **conclusion** (accept, reject, or revise) → communication/peer review.
questions.knowledgeNote: A hypothesis must be falsifiable — 'untestable explanations' are the red flag in method questions.
questions.answer: **Steps of the scientific (biological) method:** (1) **observation** of a phenomenon and collection of facts; (2) **framing a hypothesis** — a tentative, testable explanation; (3) **deduction** — predicting what should be observed if the hypothesis is true; (4) **experimentation** with a **control group** to test the deduction; (5) **recording and analysing results** (data, tables, statistics); (6) **conclusion** — accept, reject or modify the hypothesis; (7) **publication** so others can repeat and verify the work. **Deep point:** the two non-negotiables are the *testable* hypothesis and the *control* — without them an investigation is opinion, not science; publication closes the loop by inviting independent repetition.
